entries.name: IN RE TRUST UNDER AGREEMENT OF WILLIAM F. HARKINS & MARIE V. HARKINS DATED 12/3/2013, AS AMENDED

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Tom and Jaclyn's argument that Decedent would have named the special needs trusts on the form itself had he intended them to take: rejected as reading the form in isolation. The form expressly directed Fidelity to the attached letter, which unambiguously designated the Article 8-B trusts, and fn. 70 notes the language likely could not fit on the form.

Tom and Jaclyn's argument that the form names the Trust and Fidelity's records (naming the Trust without f/b/o language) control: rejected. The substantial compliance inquiry focuses on Decedent's intent and the steps Decedent took, not solely on how Fidelity recorded the designation, and Fidelity's omission does not negate those steps.

Tom and Jaclyn's argument that the instructions reflect Article 8, ¶ A, and that Article 8's opening equal-division sentence shows intent for the 4 Share Option: rejected. Reading the opening sentence in isolation obscures the distinct terms of ¶¶ A and B, and the letter unambiguously named "Article 8-B."

Jaclyn's reliance on general trust-interpretation principles (the settlor's intent as expressed in the trust instrument): rejected. Under 12 Del. C. § 602(1), a beneficiary designation is a separate instrument from a trust, and Jaclyn did not address the separate form and letter.

authorities_cited.authority: Travelers Life & Annuity Co. v. Desiderio, 2007 WL 2019795 (Del. Ch. July 3, 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: Equity may give effect to an intended beneficiary change despite failure to comply strictly with formalities. The two-element substantial compliance test applies, and expressly instructing an agent to change a beneficiary is an affirmative step.

authorities_cited.authority: Blansfield v. Alumni Ass'n of Ariz. State Univ., 2015 WL 4600802 (Del. Ch. July 31, 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: The substantial compliance doctrine applies to IRA beneficiary designations and exists to effectuate a decedent's intent where strict enforcement may work an inequity. Contrasted in fn. 51, where summary judgment was denied because the decedent never signed or returned the form.

authorities_cited.authority: Greene v. Conn. Mut. Life Ins. Co., 1977 WL 5189 (Del. Ch. May 25, 1977)
authorities_cited.proposition: Sets out the elements of substantial compliance. Strict compliance protects institutions from multiple payments and provides certainty about the proper beneficiary.

authorities_cited.authority: Emmert v. Prade, 711 A.2d 1217 (Del. Ch. 1997)
authorities_cited.proposition: An unambiguous beneficiary designation expresses the owner's intent and controls.
A beneficiary designation is an instrument or contract naming the beneficiary of specified property, distinct from an instrument creating a trust.

authorities_cited.authority: Trust Agreement art. 8 and art. 8, ¶¶ A-B
authorities_cited.proposition: Principal is divided equally, but ¶ A governs Kim's and Tom's shares and ¶ B holds Marie's and Ruth's shares in special needs trusts.

authorities_cited.authority: Fidelity Beneficiary Form and Decedent's Instruction Letter (May 20, 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Read together, these documents manifest Decedent's intent to direct 50% of the IRA to the Article 8-B special needs trusts.

authorities_cited.authority: Metro. Life Ins. Co. v. O'Donnell, 102 A. 163 (Del. 1917)
authorities_cited.proposition: Recognizes the substantial compliance doctrine for life insurance beneficiary changes.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Peierls Family Inter Vivos Trs., 77 A.3d 249 (Del. 2013) (quoting Annan v. Wilm. Tr. Co., 559 A.2d 1289 (Del. 1989))
authorities_cited.proposition: The settlor's intent controls trust interpretation. Cited in describing Jaclyn's argument, which the Court found did not reach the separate designation instruments.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 56
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment standard.
Virtual representation in trust matters.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Jeremy Paradise Dynasty Tr., 2021 WL 5564086 (Del. Ch. Nov. 29, 2021) (citing Roos v. Roos, 203 A.2d 140 (Del. Ch. 1964))
authorities_cited.proposition: Beneficiaries whose interests may be adversely affected are necessary parties to trust actions.
Govern Final Report status, the exceptions deadline and consent to final decision by a Magistrate.

summary.brief_summary: Kim, as successor trustee and executor, petitioned for instructions on whether the 50% of Decedent's Fidelity IRA payable to the Trust should go to Marie's and Ruth's special needs trusts or be split equally among all four children. Tom and his daughter Jaclyn opposed, and Kim moved for summary judgment on undisputed facts. The Magistrate in Chancery held that Delaware's substantial compliance doctrine applies to IRA beneficiary designations and that Decedent's signed form, which expressly incorporated a letter naming the "Article 8-B Trusts f/b/o" Ruth and Marie, established both intent and the affirmative steps required. Fidelity's incomplete transcription did not change the result.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether, under the substantial compliance doctrine, a decedent's Fidelity IRA beneficiary designation form (designating 50% to an "Other Entity" with "SEE ATTACHED INSTRUCTIONS") and the attached letter naming the "Article 8-B Trusts f/b/o Ruth Anne Harkins and Marie J. Harkins" effectively directed that 50% share to Marie's and Ruth's special needs trusts (the SNT Option), even though Fidelity recorded the beneficiary only as the Trust, which would otherwise require equal division among all four children (the 4 Share Option).
summary.holding: The Magistrate recommended that Kim's motion for summary judgment be granted and that Decedent's "for the benefit of" language be honored, so the 50% share passes to Marie's and Ruth's special needs trusts (the SNT Option). Both elements of substantial compliance were satisfied. First, the form and letter, read together, manifest Decedent's intent to direct that share to the Article 8-B trusts. Second, Decedent took affirmative steps: Decedent used Fidelity's prescribed form, followed its formatting instructions, signed, dated and returned it, and cross-referenced a letter identifying Marie, Ruth and the governing Trust provision. Fidelity apparently processed the letter even though it was not entirely in capitals, and no facts suggest incapacity or undue influence. Fidelity's failure to record the full designation does not negate Decedent's intent or steps. This is a Final Report under Rule 144(b)(2), and any notice of exceptions is due by November 23, 2026. The Court issued a Final Report rather than a Memorandum Opinion because not all interested parties joined the § 350/Rule 144(g) stipulation.
key_facts_and_concessions: On May 20, 2023, Decedent signed and submitted Fidelity's beneficiary designation form designating 25% to Kim, 25% to Tom, and 50% to an "Other Entity" with "SEE ATTACHED INSTRUCTIONS" in the Name field, following the form's black-ink and capital-letter instructions.

The attached letter, also dated May 20, directed Fidelity to "[p]lease [c]hange the third beneficiary to read" the "Revocable Trust of William F. Harkins and Marie V. Harkins, U/A 12/3/2013, as amended, Article 8-B Trusts f/b/o Ruth Anne Harkins and Marie J. Harkins." It addressed administration and distributions and invited Fidelity to contact Decedent with questions.

The parties do not dispute the contents of the form and letter, Fidelity's receipt of both, or Fidelity's incomplete transcription. Kim's April 20, 2026 letter stated the facts are not in dispute, only the application of law.

Fidelity's March 14, 2025 letter identified the third beneficiary as "Rev Tru Of William Marie Harkins U/A 12/[sic]." After the error was brought to its attention, Fidelity changed the name to the Trust's full name and date but omitted the "for the benefit of" language.

Trust Article 8 divides principal into equal shares for the children, but ¶ A governs Kim's and Tom's shares while ¶ B establishes special needs trusts for Marie and Ruth, of which Supportive Care Solutions, LLC is trustee.

Fidelity distributed 25% outright each to Kim and Tom and holds the remaining 50% for transfer to an Inherited IRA in the Trust's name. The IRA held about $437,798.63 at death, and the dispute is worth about $55,000 per child.
Fn. 70: the Court found it likely impossible to fit the letter's beneficiary language in the form's name field and could not do so using Fidelity's current online fillable form.

Fn. 73: Kim, Tom and Eric Merlino (as SNT trustee) stipulated to a final decision under 10 Del. C. § 350 and Rule 144(g), but Jaclyn and the three Rizzo interested parties did not. Because it was unclear the requirements were met, the Court issued a Final Report rather than a Memorandum Opinion.
summary.practical_takeaway: Where a custodian mistranscribes a beneficiary designation, a petition invoking substantial compliance can succeed on summary judgment if the owner's signed form expressly incorporates written instructions that unambiguously name the intended beneficiary and identify the governing trust provision. Petitioners seeking a final Magistrate decision should have all potentially adversely affected interested parties join the § 350/Rule 144(g) stipulation.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 56 summary judgment (no genuine issue of material fact; movant entitled to judgment as a matter of law). The proponent of substantial compliance must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) the account owner intended the change to take effect and (2) did all that was reasonably possible or necessary to effect it.

entries.name: My Carrier, LLC v. Project 44, LLC

arguments_rejected_or_waived: MyCarrier's argument that it "entirely prevailed" at arbitration on the issues litigated before the Court, and that the Final Award "confirmed" that win and entitled it to fee shifting: rejected. The Court did not read the Final Award so narrowly; the all-or-nothing provision does not permit parsing, and the panel found that no party prevailed.

MyCarrier's argument that the Final Award "can only be read as a stinging rebuke" of Project 44's theory and conduct: rejected for the same reason, because the panel concluded that no party prevailed on the merits.

MyCarrier's earlier argument that this litigation should be treated as a separate proceeding for prevailing-party purposes: rejected in the Letter Decision and not revived. Substantial overlap still dictates evaluating the proceedings as a whole.

authorities_cited.authority: MyCarrier, LLC v. Project 44, LLC, 2026 WL 191698 (Del. Ch. Jan. 21, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: The prevailing-party provision is all-or-nothing, and because there is no clean delineation between this action and the arbitration, its binary nature cautions against awarding fees before the arbitration concludes.

authorities_cited.authority: Parties' prevailing-party fee-shifting provision
authorities_cited.proposition: An all-or-nothing fee-shifting clause that does not call for parsing or allocating prevailing-party fees.

authorities_cited.authority: Arbitration panel's Final Award (Aug. 24, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Results were mixed, no party prevailed on the merits, each party bears its own fees and costs, and the Award did not distinguish this proceeding from the arbitration.

authorities_cited.authority: L&W Ins., Inc. v. Harrington, 2007 WL 1756540 (Del. Ch. June 6, 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited through the Letter Decision for the point that the arbitrator is best positioned to award fees after a final ruling on the merits.

summary.brief_summary: After the Court stayed MyCarrier, LLC's fee motion against Project 44, LLC pending arbitration of the parties' underlying dispute, the arbitration panel issued a mixed Final Award and directed each side to bear its own fees, and MyCarrier renewed its motion, arguing that it entirely prevailed on the issues litigated in Chancery. The Chancellor denied the motion by letter decision. The Chancellor held that the all-or-nothing prevailing-party clause does not permit parsing fees, that the substantial overlap between the proceedings requires assessing them as a whole, and that the panel's conclusion that no party prevailed, reached without distinguishing the two proceedings, left no basis to declare a prevailing party here.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether MyCarrier, LLC was entitled to prevailing-party fees and costs for this Court of Chancery action under an all-or-nothing fee-shifting provision, where the action substantially overlapped with a related arbitration whose Final Award produced mixed results and directed each side to bear its own fees and costs.

flags.evidence: MyCarrier argued previously that this litigation should be treated as a separate proceeding... I held in the Letter Decision, however, that... no clean delineation
flags.opinion_says: MyCarrier previously argued for separate treatment; the Court held otherwise in the Letter Decision and says the proceedings still substantially overlap and must be assessed as a whole.
flags.problem: The opinion does not say whether MyCarrier revived the argument; it only says it argued this 'previously'.

summary.holding: MyCarrier's renewed motion for attorneys' fees and costs denied. Because the prevailing-party provision is all-or-nothing and this action substantially overlapped with the arbitration without clean delineation, the prevailing-party assessment evaluates the proceedings as a whole. The arbitration panel already concluded that no party prevailed on the merits and did not distinguish between this proceeding and the arbitration in doing so. Given the substantial overlap, the Court found no basis to declare a prevailing party in this action.
key_facts_and_concessions: The arbitration panel's August 24, 2026 Final Award was mixed, with each party prevailing on some issues and losing on others; the panel concluded each party should bear its own fees and costs and denied both sides' fee requests.
The prevailing-party provision MyCarrier relies on is an all-or-nothing fee-shifting provision that does not call for parsing or allocating prevailing-party fees.
This proceeding and the arbitration substantially overlapped, with no clean delineation between them, as the Court had held in the Letter Decision.
The Final Award did not distinguish between this proceeding and the arbitration in concluding that no party prevailed on the merits.
MyCarrier acknowledged that the Final Award's results were "mixed," but contended they were "mixed only insofar as no monetary damages were awarded."

The Court's January 21, 2026 Letter Decision stayed MyCarrier's April 8, 2025 fee motion pending the arbitration, reasoning that the arbitrator would be best positioned to award fees after a final merits ruling; MyCarrier renewed the motion on September 4, 2026.
summary.practical_takeaway: Where an all-or-nothing prevailing-party clause governs a Chancery action that substantially overlaps a related arbitration, expect the Court to assess prevailing-party status across both proceedings as a whole. The Court will not carve out a win on the Chancery-litigated issues from an arbitral award that finds no party prevailed, so fee positions should be built around the overall arbitral outcome.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Plaintiff's "constant evolution" theory, that the machine-learning algorithm de-emphasized clusterin on its own: rejected as contradicted by her own verified interrogatory admission that a decision was made to exclude clusterin. Even if true, she knew of the material change and did not disclose it.

Plaintiff's argument that the switch to five biomarkers required no MolDX update because the test targeted the same indication: rejected. Even if reasonable minds could differ on MolDX requirements, the Board, not Plaintiff alone, was entitled to weigh that material risk.

Plaintiff's testimony that Capone and Fenwick authorized her deletions: found not credible and inconsistent with the documents. The deletions occurred April 21 to 23, before Fenwick's purported authorization.

Plaintiff's no-prejudice argument that she deleted only copies of documents held elsewhere and that NephroSant should have matched file names against its server: rejected. Matching file names cannot show the deleted documents were identical, and she did not return all deleted files.

Plaintiff's argument (citing Nemec) that the Confidential Information Agreement preempts the document-destruction fiduciary claim: rejected, because her duty not to destroy company information exists independently of that contract.

Plaintiff's claim to mandatory indemnification under 8 Del. C. § 145(c)(1): rejected because she was not "successful on the merits or otherwise." The Investigation targeted her conduct, she was placed on leave, the Special Committee recommended evaluating her roles, she resigned, and she only partially returned files.

NephroSant's $100 million damages claim from expert Dr. Powley: rejected. His but-for world of seamless commercialization of a six-biomarker test could never have existed because that test did not work under real-world conditions.

NephroSant's claim for $9,275,000 in PARK Study costs and for wind-down damages (restructuring legal fees, severance, lease termination): rejected. Both rested on the unproven premise that Plaintiff deleted a "Master Data File" that prevented revalidation and forced the Company's closure, and adverse inferences cannot supply that premise.

NephroSant's request for an additional $256,411.51 in Medicare and private-payor refunds: rejected (fn. 219) because NephroSant would not have received that revenue absent the breach. Its separate $2,350,000 sales and marketing claim was rejected as duplicative of the $7,125,000 award.

Plaintiff's request for adverse inferences against NephroSant for belated production and alleged concealment: denied (fn. 148). The pretrial ruling already remedied the belated production, and NephroSant did not intentionally or recklessly destroy evidence.

authorities_cited.proposition: Permissive indemnification requires good faith and a reasonable belief that the conduct was in or not opposed to the corporation's best interests. Mandatory indemnification requires success on the merits or otherwise. Neither was satisfied, which barred indemnification under the bylaws and the Indemnification Agreement as well.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Oracle Corp. Deriv. Litig., 339 A.3d 1 (Del. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Good faith requires candor with the board. Withholding material information from the board is disloyal. Materiality turns on whether a reasonable board member would regard the undisclosed facts as significant.

authorities_cited.authority: Beard Rsch., Inc. v. Kates, 981 A.2d 1175 (Del. Ch. 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: Duty to preserve on reasonable anticipation of litigation. The spoliation remedy must be tailored to culpability and prejudice; default judgment is a last resort; reckless destruction supports an adverse inference.

authorities_cited.authority: TR Invs., LLC v. Genger, 2009 WL 4696062 (Del. Ch. Dec. 9, 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: Scope of the preservation duty; the three spoliation-remedy factors (culpability, prejudice, lesser sanctions); and an award of fees and expenses related to a spoliation motion.

authorities_cited.authority: Infab Co. Inc. v. Cusick, 2024 WL 277864 (Del. Ch. Jan. 25, 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Default judgment is reserved for spoliation that renders the truth unobtainable. The equitable sanction is to draw inferences for the movant where the evidence is incomplete and it is reasonable to infer deletion. The movant does not get a blank check.

authorities_cited.authority: Sears, Roebuck & Co. v. Midcap, 893 A.2d 542 (Del. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: An adverse inference is appropriate where a litigant intentionally or recklessly destroys evidence it knows is relevant. Also applied to deny Plaintiff's request for inferences against NephroSant.

authorities_cited.authority: Equitable Tr. Co. v. Gallagher, 102 A.2d 538 (Del. 1954)
authorities_cited.proposition: Adverse inferences adopt a view of the facts as unfavorable to the wrongdoer as the known circumstances will reasonably admit. Used to limit the inference, which could not reach the Master Data File claim.

authorities_cited.authority: Kan-Di-Ki, LLC v. Suer, 2015 WL 4503210 (Del. Ch. July 22, 2015); Triton Constr. Co. v. E. Shore Elec. Servs., Inc., 2009 WL 1387115 (Del. Ch. May 18, 2009); Zbylski v. Douglas Cnty. Sch. Dist., 154 F. Supp. 3d 1146 (D. Colo. 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: The duty to preserve can attach before suit is filed, including when triggered by an internal investigation.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Saama Techs. Litig., 2026 WL 2921243 (Del. Ch. Sept. 28, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Fiduciary obligations arising from an officer role exist independently of overlapping contractual obligations, so the contract claim does not preempt the fiduciary claim.

authorities_cited.authority: Thorpe v. CERBCO, Inc., 676 A.2d 436 (Del. 1996)
authorities_cited.proposition: Directors may not compete with the corporation. Recovery for disloyalty is not determined narrowly.

authorities_cited.authority: Thorpe v. CERBCO, Inc., 1993 WL 443406 (Del. Ch. Oct. 29, 1993)
authorities_cited.proposition: Once breach is established, uncertainties in damages are resolved against the wrongdoer. Supports the $7,125,000 award as a reasonable approximation.

authorities_cited.authority: Strassburger v. Earley, 752 A.2d 557 (Del. Ch. 2000)
authorities_cited.proposition: Out-of-pocket costs that would not have been incurred but for the breach are recoverable; applied to the Fenwick investigation fees.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 37(e)
authorities_cited.proposition: Rule under which NephroSant sought spoliation sanctions.

authorities_cited.authority: Hermelin v. K-V Pharm. Co., 54 A.3d 1093 (Del. Ch. 2012)
authorities_cited.proposition: The DGCL prohibits indemnifying an unsuccessful official who acted in bad faith.

authorities_cited.authority: VonFeldt v. Stifel Fin. Corp., 1999 WL 413393 (Del. Ch. June 11, 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: Corporations lack power under § 145 to indemnify one who did not act in good faith.

authorities_cited.authority: Perconti v. Thornton Oil Corp., 2002 WL 982419 (Del. Ch. May 3, 2002)
authorities_cited.proposition: Quoted in Plaintiff's argument that success under § 145(c) entitles indemnification regardless of good faith.

authorities_cited.authority: Dodiya v. Franklin, 2026 WL 2517931 (Del. Ch. Aug. 26, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Bad faith includes acting with a purpose contrary to the corporation's interests.

authorities_cited.authority: City of Fort Myers Gen. Emps.' Pension Fund v. Haley, 235 A.3d 702 (Del. 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: Definition of materiality for board decision-making.

authorities_cited.authority: OptimisCorp v. Williams Atkins, 2026 WL 1289885 (Del. Ch. May 11, 2026); Ravenswood Inv. Co. v. Est. of Winmill, 2018 WL 1410860 (Del. Ch. Mar. 21, 2018)
authorities_cited.proposition: Nominal damages of $1 are awarded for a loyalty breach without proof of specific injury.

authorities_cited.authority: Majkowski v. Am. Imaging Mgmt. Servs., LLC, 913 A.2d 572 (Del. Ch. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Indemnification turns on the merits of the underlying controversy, so the fiduciary claim was addressed first.

authorities_cited.authority: In re J.P. Morgan Chase & Co. S'holder Litig., 906 A.2d 766 (Del. 2006); OptimisCorp v. Waite, 2015 WL 5147038 (Del. Ch. Aug. 26, 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: Damages must be logically related to the harm and may not rest on speculation.

authorities_cited.authority: Guth v. Loft, 5 A.2d 503 (Del. 1939)
authorities_cited.proposition: Fiduciaries may not use their position to further private interests.

authorities_cited.authority: Indemnification Agreement § 11(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: Presumption of entitlement to indemnification, with the burden on the Company to overcome it.

authorities_cited.authority: Sundor Elec., Inc. v. E.J.T. Constr. Co., 337 A.2d 651 (Del. 1975)
authorities_cited.proposition: Default judgment is appropriate only if no other sanction would be more appropriate.

summary.brief_summary: Founder, former CEO and director Dr. Minnie Sarwal sued NephroSant, Inc. for indemnification of expenses from a special committee investigation. NephroSant counterclaimed for breach of fiduciary duty and moved for spoliation sanctions, and the Court decided all of it after a two-day trial. The Court held Sarwal breached her duty of loyalty by withholding from the Board the decision to drop clusterin from the QSant test (described to MolDX as a six-biomarker test), by mass-deleting Box files in defiance of committee counsel's instruction, and by pitching investors on a competing venture. It awarded about $7.95 million, plus spoliation-related costs, and rejected NephroSant's $100 million but-for theory and its unsupported "Master Data File" theory. Because Sarwal acted in bad faith and was not successful in the Investigation, indemnification was neither permitted nor mandatory under § 145, foreclosing her bylaw and contract claims.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether NephroSant's founder, CEO and director breached her duty of loyalty by (i) not telling the Board that she and the CLIA lab directors had moved the QSant test from six to five biomarkers after it had been described to MolDX as a six-biomarker test, (ii) mass-deleting Company files during a special committee investigation, and (iii) soliciting investors for a competing venture. The opinion also decides what damages and spoliation sanctions follow, and whether she is entitled to indemnification under 8 Del. C. § 145, the bylaws or her Indemnification Agreement for expenses incurred in that investigation.
summary.holding:
Judgment for NephroSant on Counts I-III of the Complaint and Counts I and III of the Counterclaims. Counterclaim Count II (setoff under a promissory note) is moot, and the Court did not reach the offset argument (fn. 226).

Spoliation: the Motion for Sanctions is granted in part. Plaintiff's preservation duty attached during the Investigation, and she acted at least recklessly in mass-deleting files after Fenwick's written instruction. The sanction is that inferences will be drawn for NephroSant where the evidence is incomplete and it is reasonable to infer deletion. Default judgment was not warranted (and not sought). The request to elevate the standard of proof on affirmative defenses is moot because Plaintiff advanced none at trial. NephroSant recovers its costs of briefing the motion and of retaining a digital forensic expert; it must file a Rule 88 affidavit, and Plaintiff has 30 days to respond.

Liability: Plaintiff breached her duty of loyalty three ways:
- concealing the five-biomarker change from the Board, likely because she feared disclosure would impede progress and financing;
- destroying Company documents, more likely than not to impede an Investigation focused on her conduct;
- soliciting investors for a competing venture.
NephroSant did not prove whistleblower retaliation (fn. 167), and did not prove that a foundational "Master Data File" was deleted or necessitated the PARK Study.

Damages: $7,125,000 for costs of developing and marketing the unapproved five-biomarker test from April 2021 to April 2022, $827,682.84 in Investigation fees, and $1 in nominal damages for the solicitation, totaling $7,952,683.84. The $100 million but-for claim, PARK Study and wind-down costs, Medicare refunds and duplicative marketing costs are rejected.

Indemnification: denied. Plaintiff's bad faith bars permissive indemnification under § 145(a), she was not successful under § 145(c)(1), and indemnification therefore is unavailable under the bylaws or the Indemnification Agreement.
key_facts_and_concessions: Plaintiff's verified interrogatory responses conceded that, in weekly R/D meetings with the CLIA lab directors, "a decision was made to exclude a marker, Clusterin" because of heat degradation risk during shipping. Ghosh testified the algorithm was "locked" at five biomarkers by April 2021, while MolDX submissions continued to describe a six-biomarker test.

Plaintiff, a director, did not inform her fellow directors of the change (PTO ¶ 93). The Board learned of it only in April 2022, after employees raised concerns following her March 2022 step-down as CEO.

On April 21, 2022, Special Committee counsel Fenwick directed Plaintiff in writing to refrain from deleting or altering her NephroSant Box account. Between April 21 and 23 she downloaded about 33,000 files, "double deleted" about 15,000, and had her son Reuben Sarwal delete documents. She admitted she deleted "the whole folder" rather than reviewing file by file for HIPAA-protected material.

NephroSant first referred to a foundational "Main Data File" (later "Master Data File") in its May 2026 pre-trial brief and could not describe it with specificity. Ghosh's Initial Validation in late April and early May 2022 used the Nolan, Wanzin and EAP data.

NephroSant's post-trial brief conceded it would have had to "resolve the stability issues with the 6 biomarker algorithm" to use that test (fn. 210). The Court found the six-biomarker test did not work as expected under real-world conditions.

In late May 2022, Plaintiff suggested to NephroSant investors (including Alireza and Magee) that they back a new venture, saying the IP would revert to UCSF if NephroSant went bankrupt. Nothing came of it, and NephroSant conceded at post-trial argument that damages from this breach were "minimal."
The record showed NephroSant spent at least $7,125,000 developing and marketing the QSant test from April 2021 through April 2022, and incurred $827,682.84 in Fenwick fees for the Investigation.

Plaintiff did not advance any affirmative defenses at trial (fn. 135), and she waived Count III of the Complaint (breach of Indemnification Agreement § 9(b)) by not addressing it in post-trial briefing (fn. 118).
summary.practical_takeaway: A fiduciary who believes a material product change needs no regulatory disclosure must still put it before the board, and once an internal investigation begins should not bulk-delete files, even ones claimed to hold HIPAA-protected or third-party material, without a document-by-document review. Companies pursuing spoliation should identify early and specifically what data was lost and how its loss caused the claimed harm, and build damages on a realistic but-for world, because adverse inferences will not supply missing causal proof.
summary.standard_of_review: Post-trial; preponderance of the evidence. NephroSant bore the burden on each element of its fiduciary duty counterclaim, including damages, and, under Indemnification Agreement § 11(a), the burden to overcome the presumption that Plaintiff was entitled to indemnification. Spoliation sanctions under Ct. Ch. R. 37(e) turned on culpability, prejudice and the availability of lesser sanctions, and must be just and reasonable.
